policy: The v1.8.3 contract is frozen: each active source's URL building, list parsing and JD fetch live in jobs_scraper/sources/<source>.py, and sg_product_jobs.py keeps only thin wrappers over them — one implementation per behaviour, verified by AST. The active CLI sources are linkedin, jobstreet, cake and 104/onezerofour; jora stays retired from active crawling and is kept only for back-compat dedup of historical rows. Every source adapter's list fetch retries a transient 429/5xx/connection/JSON failure with a 30/60/90s ladder (four attempts), raises any other 4xx without retrying, and never retries a legitimately empty page; a run counts as successful only when the list crawl actually produced pages, because an empty crawl exits 0 by design. A legitimately empty LinkedIn list page is 26 bytes and yields no parseable root: the list parser returns zero jobs for it instead of raising, so one empty page can never end a page loop, a chunk or a run. The LinkedIn JD fetch uses the same 30/60/90s ladder (four attempts) for a 429, a 5xx or a connection error, and does not retry any other 4xx, because a job whose JD never arrives is skipped by the Sheet writer and would otherwise disappear from the run silently. Code that generates a Python worker embeds its arguments as Python literals, never as JSON: json.dumps(None) is the bare token null, an undefined name in Python, and such a worker dies before it reaches Google and silently costs the run the subprocess timeout guard that protects the Sheet write. A generated worker never carries the jobs payload in its source: the payload travels in a separate JSON file the worker reads, because a source that embeds it grows to megabytes and makes CPython pull the whole literal through its tokenizer before the write can start, which is a memory spike on a machine whose free-page count is already in the tens of megabytes. The engine's title filter, Sheet write order, cross-source identity, work-mode values and single-source-of-truth crawl state are unchanged by this release; future source expansion or retirement requires an explicit authorized contract change. Outbound proxy resolution lives in one place, jobs_scraper.sources.resolve_proxies(), and every adapter that talks to a third party uses it: JOBS_SCRAPER_PROXY first, then the standard HTTPS_PROXY / HTTP_PROXY / ALL_PROXY, and nothing set means a direct connection; no source may reach for a proxy variable of its own. The doctor reports which proxy is in effect and probes whether it is still reachable, because a configured-but-dead proxy fails every source at once. China is three crawlable places, not one: the China region is Shanghai, and Hangzhou and Shenzhen are their own regions with verified LinkedIn geoIds in the LinkedIn adapter's preset table. A region resolves its Sheet tab through a tab-base rule, so the two city regions land on China-Raw / China-Selected together with the China region, and the expected-tab list is de-duplicated so the initializer never creates a shared tab twice; the city regions stay opt-in and the default region set remains SG / TW / China. A China posting carries no visa judgement: China-specific citizenship wording produces no signal, because a Taiwan resident can take a permit into mainland China. The generic coverage stays — a Singapore or Taiwan posting that requires any citizenship is still a hard blocker, and the Singapore-only gate on the Sheet's visa column is unchanged. The pre-detail dedup reads the tab the run is about to write to: the target gid is resolved with the same precedence the writer uses — explicit --gid, then the #gid= inside --to-sheet, then the source-label mapping — and it is threaded into the loader, into the generated worker and into main(); a label-to-gid table alone is not a target, because LinkedIn / Minimax points at SG-Raw, so a China run compared its postings against Singapore's tab and paid for a JD fetch round the writer was going to discard. With no target given, the label-to-gid mapping still applies, so the Singapore and Taiwan flows behave exactly as before, and an explicit target is authoritative without needing a known label. A range's page budget must cover the pool that range actually has in every known city, not only the city it was measured in first: the LinkedIn budgets are pinned to the deepest measured pool per range across Shanghai and Singapore, and the JobStreet budgets are pinned to the totals the JobStreet API states for itself, sized for the largest keyword's pool plus headroom — the JobStreet daterange parameter takes a number of days, mapped through JOBSTREET_TPR, never the CLI range name. Every JobStreet keyword is crawled to the end of its own pool: the soft stop that ends a keyword measures the postings that are new to that keyword, never the postings that are new to the whole crawl, because the five keywords share one seen set and a signal measured against that set stops four of the five keywords on their first page. The shared set decides only what is returned, so a posting two keywords both match is still returned once, and the JobStreet page budget is sized for the largest keyword's pool. A keyword that exhausts its retries ends that keyword only: the failure stays visible while the other keywords' postings are not discarded with it. Every JobStreet keyword is crawled to the end of its own pool: the soft stop that ends a keyword measures the postings that are new to that keyword, never the postings that are new to the whole crawl, because the five keywords share one seen set and a signal measured against that set stops four of the five keywords on their first page. The shared set decides only what is returned, so a posting two keywords both match is still returned once, and the JobStreet page budget is sized for the largest keyword's pool. A keyword that exhausts its retries ends that keyword only: the failure stays visible while the other keywords' postings are not discarded with it. No budget ever shrinks and no time filter ever changes. The Guest API refuses to paginate past start=1000: it answers HTTP 400 rather than an empty page, so a budget beyond 100 pages buys nothing and a crawl that asks for an unreachable page ends with what it collected instead of aborting — the ceiling is an end, not a failure, and a supervisor never reads it as a coverage gap. A non-429 4xx on a LinkedIn list page is raised immediately as FatalListPageError, exactly as the JobStreet adapter does, because the retry ladder is for transient failures and a caller bug only burns the backoff ladder. A source that talks to a third party sends the request the way a browser would: the 104 adapter now carries the sec-fetch-dest / sec-fetch-mode / sec-fetch-site header group, x-requested-with and Origin, because without them 104's jobs search API answers 403 while its homepage answers 200 — and it passes the same shared proxy resolution as every other adapter, because a direct request is refused as well. The symptom of getting this wrong is an empty crawl rather than an error, which is why a source-specific bot-protection requirement is part of the source's contract. A Sheet write never overwrites a row that holds data: the write start is resolved once the number of rows is known, and a blank row in the middle of the sheet is reused only when the whole write fits into blank rows, otherwise the run appends at the end. The opposite happened on 2026-11-24: a run that wrote 159 rows into a one-row hole destroyed 415 rows of collected jobs, and those jobs were then fetched again because they were no longer in the sheet to be de-duplicated against. Every source owns its own request pacing, and the adapter is where that budget lives: the JobStreet adapter paces at 0.5-1.0s, the LinkedIn adapter at 1.5-3.0s, Cake stays at 3-10s. Measured 2026-11-24: the pure network time of a JobStreet list page is 0.80s, of a JobStreet JD 0.29s, of a LinkedIn list page 0.92s, while the old 3-10s sleep between every request made 80% of a run's wall time waiting. The engine keeps one sleep injection point and the source being crawled selects the range through a context variable, so a test that replaces the sleep replaces every source's pacing and a worker thread has to set the source itself. A budget can be overridden from the environment without touching the code; a malformed value falls back to the default and an inverted range is swapped, never rejected. The retry ladders are unchanged by the pacing change. A crawl may be given a page span (--start-page / --max-pages) and a chunk that owns a span crawls only its own pages: the cumulative style re-crawled every earlier page on every chunk, which cost 2,179 page fetches for a 30d JobStreet pool that needs about 406, a 5.4x redundancy, and 355 for a 100-page LinkedIn pool, a 3.55x one. Consecutive spans cover every page exactly once, and cross-chunk de-duplication does not depend on the span because the seen file plus the pre-detail dedup against the target tab both survive across processes. --start-page defaults to 1, so a crawl without a span behaves exactly as before, and a span that lies beyond the pool returns no data, which is an end rather than a gap. Detail fetches run in a thread pool; the threads do network I/O and nothing else, so the seen file, the counters and the output order are the main thread's, and a worker count of 1 keeps the fully sequential behaviour. The 104 list budget is chosen by aggregate request rate rather than by the gap between one request and the next, because 104's list API is sensitive to how many requests are in flight: eight keyword workers at 1.0-2.0s each is an aggregate 2.1 req/s and was answered with 403 at the start of a run, while a single worker at 1.0-2.0s is an aggregate 0.5-1.0 req/s and walked 50 pages with zero failures. One keyword in flight uses the 104 budget and several keywords in flight keep the global budget, and the source is pinned inside the adapter's own worker thread, because a context variable set in the main thread is invisible in a worker. The crawl supervisors live in the repository under ops/ and are part of this frozen baseline, because the rules above about how a supervisor treats a span beyond the pool, which keys the state file holds, and which chunk keys are recorded as done are the supervisors' own behaviour. A supervisor resolves its paths from the environment and never carries a spreadsheet id, a service-account identity or a private key: the repository's hygiene guard scans the whole tracked tree for exactly those, and the China runners fail closed when no spreadsheet id is configured. The plugin runtime receives the repository's ops/ directory on every sync, because the crawl supervisors in there are frozen baseline behaviour and a runtime that kept a private copy of them would run behaviour the baseline does not describe. The sync manifest itself is part of the frozen baseline, because it is the mechanism that gives the upstream repository, the plugin runtime and a working copy the same bytes for every tracked file; it merges directories rather than replacing them, never deletes a file the local side owns alone, and never touches the Mavis-specific files or the private runtime state on its preserve list. The sync carries the frozen supervisors but does not run them: a crawl is launched from the repository checkout and the runtime directory holds only logs and state, so exactly one copy of a supervisor can be launched.
